Description

CB2 is the cannabinoid receptor of immune cells, and its presence on sensory neurons is still debated, although mouse genetics points to a role in nociceptors. Activated by endocannabinoids, CB2 signals through Gi to inhibit adenylate cyclase. In rat models of OA, CB2 agonists reduce pain and spinal sensitisation, but in human hand OA cannabidiol did not reduce pain.

Colour

Proteins and metabolites are coloured by their contribution to pain: red for those that raise it (they excite or sensitise nociceptive neurons, or drive the inflammation that does), blue for those that relieve it, and olive for the shared signalling machinery (G proteins, RGS, adenylate cyclase, phospholipases, kinases, adaptors, second messengers, ions and nucleotides), whose effect is set by the receptor upstream. Metabolites take a lighter shade of the same colour. Drugs are yellow and classes of molecules white. Each molecule is coloured by its role in this block, so the same molecule can be red in one block and blue in another.

Cannabinoids and CB2 are blue. Activating CB2 relieves pathological pain with few central side effects (Guindon 2008) and, on mast cells and other immune cells, decreases the release of pro-inflammatory mediators (Pini 2012), so its actions on pain and on inflammation agree.
